name: Peeso (Estonian Horns)
description: Peeso is a popular Estonian social game, often described as a regional folk variant of the game '6 nimmt!'. Players simultaneous play cards into four rows on the table, following strict rules of ascending order and 'smallest difference'. If a player is forced to place the 6th card in a row, they must take the entire row as penalty points (called 'Sarved' or Horns). It is a game of risk management, psychological anticipation, and avoidant scoring.

history.origins: Derived from Central European 'Cow' and 'Bull' games, it found a unique cultural home in Estonia where it is often associated with the 'Sarved' (Horns) folk imagery.
timeline: 20th Century: Variations of horizontal-row card games spread through the Baltic states.
1990s: Peeso is standardized alongside the popularity of German 'Amigo' style card games.
2000s: Becomes a staple in Estonian social clubs and family gatherings.
Present: Highly recognized as a fun, 'mean' game of luck and timing.
history.cultural: To 'Get the Horns' in Peeso is a humorous idiom for making a tactical error that benefits everyone else while hurting yourself.
history.evolution: The transition from standard 52-card decks to numbered decks allowed for more players and higher tension in the 'Smallest Difference' calculation.

setup.deck: 104 cards numbered 1 to 104. Each card has a certain number of 'Horns' (points).
setup.dealing: Each player gets 10 cards. Four cards are placed face-up in a vertical column to start the four rows.

rules.objective: Score the fewest points (Horns) by the end of the game.
rules.gameplay: Each turn all players simultaneously choose one card and reveal them together. Cards are placed in ascending order onto one of four table rows: each card goes on the row whose end card is lower than the played card and closest in value (smallest difference). If a card is the 6th on a row, the player takes the five existing cards as penalty (Horns) and their card starts a new row. If the played card is lower than all row ends, the player chooses a row to take and their card starts that row. After 10 turns the round ends; players sum their Horn points. The game ends when someone reaches 66 or more points; the player with the fewest total points wins.
keyRules: Play one card per turn simultaneously; cards resolved from lowest to highest.
Place card on the row where the end card is lower than your card and closest in value.
Placing the 6th card on a row: take the five cards as penalty (Horns), your card starts the row.
If your card is lower than all four row ends, choose a row to take; your card starts that row.
Game ends when a player reaches 66 or more total Horn points; lowest total wins.

strategy.basic: Avoid the 'Danger' rows. If a row already has 5 cards, do not play a card that is just slightly higher than the 5th cardâ€”you will almost certainly be forced to take it. Instead, play a very high card that will land in a 'Short' row, or a very low card to 'Flush' a low-point row if you know you are going to lose anyway.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Hole' Play: If you have a sequence (e.g., 22, 23, 24), you can safely play them over multiple turns if the last number in a row is something like 20. Because you know nobody else can play a card BETWEEN 20 and 22, you won't be pushed into the 6th spot by an opponent. Create your own safe gaps.
strategy.advanced: Crowd-Psychology Blocking: In a 10-player game, rows fill up instantly. If you see many players are low on cards, they will likely play high. Use this to your advantage by playing consistently low, forcing THEM to take the 10-point rows while you take a single 1-point card to reset a row early. Knowing when to 'take a small hit' to avoid a 'massive blowout' is the key to winning Peeso.
tips: Cards ending in 5 or 0, and double numbers (like 55), usually have more 'Horns' (points). Avoid taking these at all costs.
Calculated Suicide: If you have to take a row, pick the one with the fewest points, even if it's not the one your card technically belonged to (if you were too low to play anywhere else).
